The density at the center of the star is higher than that in atomic nuclei. As a result, the properties of neutron stars provide important information about the behavior of ordinary matter under extreme compression. In recent years, new information about neutron stars has emerged from two sources. The first is the observation of the gravitational-wave signal from the final inspiral of a coalescing binary neutron star. The second is a careful measurement of the x-ray pulse profile of a spinning neutron star. This review discusses these measurements and summarizes how they constrain masses, radii, and central densities. The results are compared to predictions based on calculations of the nuclear equation of state at densities comparable to that in atomic nuclei, which are then extrapolated to higher density. The review ends with an outlook on future observational opportunities.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045007] Published Wed Dec 24, 2025.
tldr: A review of neutron star observations and the dense matter equation of state, focusing on gravitational-wave and X-ray measurements.
motivation: To understand the behavior of matter at extreme densities found in neutron stars, which is crucial for nuclear physics and astrophysics.
method: Review of observational data from gravitational-wave events (binary neutron star mergers) and X-ray pulse profile measurements, compared to theoretical predictions of the nuclear equation of state.
result: Constraints on neutron star masses, radii, and central densities are summarized, showing consistency with some nuclear models but leaving uncertainties at high densities.
conclusion: Future observations will further refine the equation of state, but current data already provide important insights into dense matter.

title: Spin-glass Dynamics: Experiment, Theory, And Simulation
authors: E. D. Dahlberg, I. González-Adalid Pemartín, E. Marinari, G. Parisi, F. Ricci-Tersenghi, V. Martin-Mayor, J. Moreno-Gordo, R. L. Orbach, I. Paga, J. J. Ruiz-Lorenzo, And D. Yllanes
abstract:
Author(s): E. D. Dahlberg, I. González-Adalid Pemartín, E. Marinari, G. Parisi, F. Ricci-Tersenghi, V. Martin-Mayor, J. Moreno-Gordo, R. L. Orbach, I. Paga, J. J. Ruiz-Lorenzo, and D. Yllanes

This review updates the field of spin glasses with broad application to a large variety of physical systems. In particular, this review tracks the progress of experiment, theory, and large-scale simulations. It highlights the importance of their synergy, from the inception of the field to the present day, and includes future opportunities for research.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045005] Published Mon Dec 15, 2025.
tldr: A review of spin-glass dynamics covering experiment, theory, and simulation.
motivation: To provide an updated overview of spin-glass research and highlight the synergy between experiment, theory, and simulation.
method: Review of experimental, theoretical, and computational studies of spin glasses.
result: Summarizes progress in understanding spin-glass dynamics and identifies future research opportunities.
conclusion: Spin-glass research continues to be relevant for a variety of physical systems, and interdisciplinary approaches are essential.

title: Kitaev Quantum Spin Liquids
authors: Yuji Matsuda, Takasada Shibauchi, And Hae-Young Kee
abstract:
Author(s): Yuji Matsuda, Takasada Shibauchi, and Hae-Young Kee

Frustration in spin systems can prevent ordering even at =0, creating quantum spin liquids that have been sought since Anderson’s pioneering work in 1973 and his influential 1987 paper connecting them to high-temperature superconductivity. Kitaev’s solvable spin-1/2 models on a honeycomb lattice brought renewed attention to this field, with Jackeli and Khaliullin later revealing how to engineer Kitaev interactions in real materials. This review highlights theoretical and experimental developments in Kitaev spin liquids, emphasizing leading candidate materials and their broad topological properties such as chiral edge modes. Consequently, it provides essential insights for both experimentalists and theorists working on quantum spin liquid problems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045003] Published Wed Dec 03, 2025.
tldr: A review of Kitaev quantum spin liquids, focusing on candidate materials and topological properties.
motivation: To provide an overview of theoretical and experimental progress in Kitaev spin liquids, which are a type of quantum spin liquid with potential applications in topological quantum computing.
method: Review of theoretical models (Kitaev honeycomb model) and experimental studies on candidate materials, highlighting chiral edge modes and other topological features.
result: Summarizes key candidate materials and their properties, emphasizing the realization of Kitaev interactions and the observation of topological phenomena.
conclusion: Kitaev spin liquids are a rich field with promising materials, but further work is needed to confirm quantum spin liquid behavior and explore applications.

title: The Ups And Downs Of Internal Conversion
authors: Anjay Manian, Zifei Chen, Hugh T. Sullivan, And Salvy P. Russo
abstract:
Author(s): Anjay Manian, Zifei Chen, Hugh T. Sullivan, and Salvy P. Russo

This review examines the theoretical methods used to describe the photophysical process of internal conversion in quantum systems. These models explore all facets of the nonradiative mechanism, and the review presents an outlook on how they can be incorporated in studies relevant to applications, for example, in photonics and energy harvesting.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 035003] Published Tue Sep 16, 2025.
tldr: A review of theoretical methods for internal conversion in quantum systems, focusing on nonradiative transitions and their applications in photonics and energy harvesting.
motivation: Internal conversion is a key photophysical process, and understanding its theoretical underpinnings is important for applications in photonics and energy harvesting.
method: The paper reviews various theoretical models describing internal conversion, including nonradiative mechanisms and their incorporation into application-relevant studies.
result: The review provides an overview of current theoretical methods and an outlook on future directions for integrating these models into practical applications.
conclusion: Theoretical methods for internal conversion are advancing, but further development is needed to fully exploit them in photonics and energy harvesting.

title: Colloquium: Quantum Properties And Functionalities Of Magnetic Skyrmions
authors: Alexander P. Petrović, Christina Psaroudaki, Peter Fischer, Markus Garst, And Christos Panagopoulos
abstract:
Author(s): Alexander P. Petrović, Christina Psaroudaki, Peter Fischer, Markus Garst, and Christos Panagopoulos

Skyrmions are topological field configurations that were first discussed in the context of high-energy theory. In recent years, skyrmionic spin patterns in solid-state systems have received much attention, in part for their promising application potential. This Colloquium discusses quantum-mechanical aspects of such magnetic skyrmions, both for the interactions that underlie skyrmion formation and for quantum features of the skyrmions themselves.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 031001] Published Tue Jul 08, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews quantum properties and functionalities of magnetic skyrmions, focusing on their topological nature and potential applications.
motivation: Magnetic skyrmions are promising for spintronic devices, but their quantum aspects are less explored; this review aims to bridge that gap.
method: The paper surveys theoretical and experimental work on skyrmion formation, quantum interactions, and quantum features of skyrmions themselves.
result: It highlights quantum-mechanical effects in skyrmion systems, such as quantum tunneling and entanglement, and discusses their potential for quantum technologies.
conclusion: Quantum skyrmions may enable new functionalities in quantum information processing, but the field is still nascent with many open questions.

title: Order And Disorder At The Atomic Scale: Microscopy Applied To Semiconductors
authors: Enrico Di Russo, Tom Verstijnen, Paul Koenraad, Konstantinos Pantzas, Gilles Patriarche, And Lorenzo Rigutti
abstract:
Author(s): Enrico Di Russo, Tom Verstijnen, Paul Koenraad, Konstantinos Pantzas, Gilles Patriarche, and Lorenzo Rigutti

Atomic-scale details, especially those of disorder, are important for material properties, especially in semiconductors, but they are also extremely difficult to measure. Real-space methods can give direct access to this information, but typically, that access is limited. This review reports the application of three real-space techniques for measuring disorder to compound semiconductor materials: scanning tunneling microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and atom-probe microscopy. Where possible, it emphasizes cases in which the probes have been combined to achieve a more complete picture of the defects.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025006] Published Thu Jun 26, 2025.
tldr: A review of real-space microscopy techniques for measuring atomic-scale disorder in semiconductors.
motivation: Atomic-scale disorder critically affects semiconductor properties but is difficult to measure; the paper aims to review three complementary real-space techniques.
method: The authors review scanning tunneling microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and atom-probe microscopy, emphasizing combined use for a complete picture of defects.
result: The review highlights how each technique provides unique information about disorder and how combining them yields a more comprehensive understanding.
conclusion: Real-space microscopy techniques, especially when combined, are powerful tools for characterizing atomic-scale disorder in semiconductors.

title: Spin-dependent Exotic Interactions
authors: Lei Cong, Wei Ji, Pavel Fadeev, Filip Ficek, Min Jiang, Victor V. Flambaum, Haosen Guan, Derek F. Jackson Kimball, Mikhail G. Kozlov, Yevgeny V. Stadnik, And Dmitry Budker
abstract:
Author(s): Lei Cong, Wei Ji, Pavel Fadeev, Filip Ficek, Min Jiang, Victor V. Flambaum, Haosen Guan, Derek F. Jackson Kimball, Mikhail G. Kozlov, Yevgeny V. Stadnik, and Dmitry Budker

This review presents a comprehensive summary of theoretical investigations and experimental searches for spin-dependent interactions beyond the standard model. These interactions may be mediated by various types of exotic bosons, and their existence and properties may, in turn, explain the nature of dark matter and dark energy. The described experiments also probe the discrete fundamental symmetries of nature.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025005] Published Tue Jun 24, 2025.
tldr: A comprehensive review of theoretical and experimental searches for spin-dependent exotic interactions beyond the standard model, including their possible connection to dark matter and dark energy.
motivation: To understand the nature of dark matter and dark energy and to probe discrete fundamental symmetries through spin-dependent interactions mediated by exotic bosons.
method: The paper reviews theoretical models of spin-dependent exotic interactions and summarizes experimental searches using various techniques such as atomic magnetometry, torsion balances, and astrophysical observations.
result: The review catalogs current constraints on coupling constants and interaction ranges for various exotic boson mediators, highlighting the most sensitive experiments and remaining parameter space.
conclusion: Spin-dependent exotic interactions remain a promising avenue for discovering new physics, but no definitive evidence has been found; future experiments with improved sensitivity are needed.

title: Colloquium: Materials That Exceed Classical Thermodynamic Bounds On Properties
authors: Roderic S. Lakes
abstract:
Author(s): Roderic S. Lakes

Classical thermodynamic bounds provide constraints on values that are expected in measurements of certain physical properties. In a variety of fields, some measurements exceed these bounds. This apparent violation of thermodynamics arises because the measurements are made in ways that violate the underlying assumptions made when deriving these bounds. This Colloquium describes a wide variety of circumstances where such violations occur and which of the underlying assumptions are violated in each case. It also describes how interesting material properties can be developed using materials designed to violate these assumptions.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 021002] Published Wed May 14, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews materials that appear to exceed classical thermodynamic bounds on properties, explaining the violations by examining underlying assumptions.
motivation: Classical thermodynamic bounds are often assumed to be fundamental, but some measurements exceed them; understanding why can lead to new materials with enhanced properties.
method: The paper surveys a wide variety of materials and phenomena where bounds are exceeded, analyzing which assumptions (e.g., equilibrium, linearity, homogeneity) are violated.
result: It identifies that violations occur when measurements are made in ways that violate assumptions such as equilibrium, linear response, or spatial homogeneity, and shows how designed materials can exploit these violations.
conclusion: Apparent violations of thermodynamic bounds are not actual violations but arise from misapplication of bounds; this insight can guide the development of materials with extreme properties.

title: Colloquium: Synthetic Quantum Matter In Nonstandard Geometries
authors: Tobias Grass, Dario Bercioux, Utso Bhattacharya, Maciej Lewenstein, Hai Son Nguyen, And Christof Weitenberg
abstract:
Author(s): Tobias Grass, Dario Bercioux, Utso Bhattacharya, Maciej Lewenstein, Hai Son Nguyen, and Christof Weitenberg

This Colloquium presents ways to implement fractal lattices, curved spaces, and higher dimensions in atomic, photonic, and electronic systems. The study of quantum many-body physics in these exotic geometries permits simulation of phenomena from topology in condensed matter to models of gravity and cosmology.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 011001] Published Tue Mar 25, 2025.
tldr: A colloquium review on implementing fractal lattices, curved spaces, and higher dimensions in atomic, photonic, and electronic systems for quantum many-body physics.
motivation: To explore exotic geometries that enable simulation of phenomena from condensed matter topology to gravity and cosmology.
method: Review of experimental and theoretical approaches for realizing nonstandard geometries in various quantum platforms.
result: Summarizes current capabilities and challenges in simulating quantum matter on fractal lattices, curved spaces, and higher dimensions.
conclusion: These synthetic quantum systems offer a promising route to study fundamental physics beyond standard geometries.

title: Massive Quantum Systems As Interfaces Of Quantum Mechanics And Gravity
authors: Sougato Bose, Ivette Fuentes, Andrew A. Geraci, Saba Mehsar Khan, Sofia Qvarfort, Markus Rademacher, Muddassar Rashid, Marko Toroš, Hendrik Ulbricht, And Clara C. Wanjura
abstract:
Author(s): Sougato Bose, Ivette Fuentes, Andrew A. Geraci, Saba Mehsar Khan, Sofia Qvarfort, Markus Rademacher, Muddassar Rashid, Marko Toroš, Hendrik Ulbricht, and Clara C. Wanjura

The authors review theories and experimental state-of-the-art efforts to study the effects of gravity on massive quantum systems. Classical gravity is the least precisely tested natural force and may be addressed via precision quantum probes. Experiments testing whether the quantum nature of gravity causes decoherence and collapse of matter-wave functions and whether it can mediate entanglement between separate massive particles are underway, and their results will guide the theoretical description of gravity effects on a laboratory scale.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015003] Published Thu Feb 13, 2025.
tldr: A review of experimental and theoretical efforts to probe gravity using massive quantum systems, focusing on decoherence and entanglement mediated by gravity.
motivation: Classical gravity is the least precisely tested natural force, and quantum probes may reveal its quantum nature.
method: The paper reviews theories of gravity-induced decoherence and collapse, and ongoing experiments with massive quantum systems to test these effects.
result: Current experiments are exploring whether gravity causes decoherence or can mediate entanglement between massive particles.
conclusion: Results from these experiments will guide the theoretical description of gravity on a laboratory scale.

title: Observation Of Alignment Tensor Effects In Metastability-exchange Collisions With Highly Polarized 3 ...
authors: Yida Sha, Kaiwen Yi, Xingqing Jin, Matteo Fadel And Xiang Peng
abstract: Highly polarized ensembles prepared by metastability-exchange optical pumping (MEOP) have been widely used in precision measurements and fundamental physics. Metastability-exchange (ME) collisions, serving as the basis of MEOP, are traditionally described in terms of atomic orientation, while the significant contributions of metastable alignment tensor at high polarization remain unexplored. In this work, we develop a linearized model under mean-field approximation to investigate alignment tensor effects in highly polarized , which originate from the metastable manifold and are revealed through ME-induced relaxation and frequency shift. By means of free-induction-decay measurements, a pronounced dependence on nuclear polarization is experimentally observed in the response of the ground-state-metastable hybrid ensembles to the external magnetic field. Furthermore, after obtaining the characteristics of tensor-induced phenomena, we demonstrate good agreement between the experiment and the theory. This work advances the understanding of nuclear spin dynamics in highly polarized using MEOP. It further provides applications in systematic error correction of high-accuracy magnetometry, as well as in optimal protocol for the generation of nuclear spin-squeezed states.
tldr: This paper studies alignment tensor effects in metastability-exchange collisions for highly polarized 3He, focusing on nuclear spin dynamics and magnetometry applications.
motivation: To understand alignment tensor contributions in metastability-exchange optical pumping at high polarization, which are not captured by traditional orientation-based models.
method: Develops a linearized mean-field model and validates it with free-induction-decay measurements on hybrid ground-state-metastable ensembles.
result: Observes a pronounced dependence of the ensemble response on nuclear polarization, and achieves good agreement between theory and experiment.
conclusion: Advances understanding of nuclear spin dynamics in highly polarized 3He and provides applications for systematic error correction in magnetometry and generation of spin-squeezed states.

title: Strain-driven Transition From Correlated Insulating To Semimetallic States In Twisted-bilayer Graphene
authors: Lishuai Guo, Abulimiti Yasen, Mei Xiang, Wenliang Zhu And Minghu Pan
abstract: We investigate the interplay between Coulomb interaction and uniaxial heterostrain in twisted bilayer graphene (TBG) using a self-consistent Hartree–Fock (HF) approach projected onto the flat bands. For integer filling factors in the range of , we find that heterostrain strongly reconstructs the low-energy band structure and suppresses interaction-induced insulating gaps. As strain magnitude increases, the flat-band bandwidth is substantially enhanced, leading to an increased kinetic energy. The bandwidth enhancement effectively weakens the interaction strength relative to kinetic energy, resulting in the suppression of HF gaps and the emergence of semimetallic (SM) states. The strain effect can be primarily controlled by the filling factor, as well as the strain direction. At moderate strain strengths around 0.3% for , it can drive transitions between correlated insulating and SM states. In contrast, for , the HF gaps becomes negligible and the system remains essentially SM; both the strain direction and magnitude have negligible influence. Our results demonstrate that uniaxial heterostrain serves as an effective and versatile parameter for tuning correlated phases in TBG through the interplay of lattice deformation and Coulomb interactions.
tldr: This paper studies strain-driven transitions between correlated insulating and semimetallic states in twisted bilayer graphene using Hartree-Fock calculations.
motivation: Understanding how uniaxial heterostrain affects correlated phases in twisted bilayer graphene, which is a key material in condensed matter physics.
method: Self-consistent Hartree-Fock approach projected onto flat bands to compute band structure and interaction-induced gaps under varying strain.
result: Heterostrain enhances bandwidth, suppresses insulating gaps, and drives transitions to semimetallic states; effect depends on filling factor and strain direction.
conclusion: Uniaxial heterostrain is an effective tuning parameter for correlated phases in twisted bilayer graphene.

title: Observation Of Floquet Tensor Monopoles
authors: Hao Yuan, Weixuan Zhang, Na Sun And Xiangdong Zhang
abstract: Tensor monopoles, topological singularities of Kalb–Ramond tensor gauge fields, have garnered widespread attention in high-energy and condensed matter physics. They give rise to exotic phenomena such as quantized magnetoelectric responses and chiral boundary states, acting as potential building blocks for the development of topological devices in high-dimensional space. However, theoretical studies and experimental realizations reported to date have remained in static settings, and the realization of Floquet tensor monopoles (FTMs) and their associated anomalous non-equilibrium topological features has yet to be achieved. Here, we report the first theoretical and experimental implementation of FTMs in a four-dimensional non-equilibrium system. We systematically uncover the driving-frequency controlled creation, motion, and annihilation of FTMs, together with their anomalous bulk-edge correspondence. These phenomena are unique to FTMs and have no static counterparts. In experiments, we design and fabricate time-varying topological circuits, and directly observe the controllable motion of FTMs in k-space and their induced 3D Fermi-arc surface states by tuning the driving frequency. Our findings extend tensor monopole research to the non-equilibrium regime, providing a theoretical and experimental platform for exploring exotic topological phases in dynamic tensor gauge fields and laying the groundwork for functional topological devices with real-time control.
tldr: This paper reports the first experimental observation of Floquet tensor monopoles in a four-dimensional non-equilibrium system, demonstrating their creation, motion, and annihilation controlled by driving frequency.
motivation: Tensor monopoles have been studied in static settings, but their non-equilibrium counterparts (Floquet tensor monopoles) and associated anomalous topological features had not been realized.
method: The authors design and fabricate time-varying topological circuits to realize a four-dimensional non-equilibrium system, and observe the controllable motion of Floquet tensor monopoles in momentum space and their induced 3D Fermi-arc surface states by tuning the driving frequency.
result: They observe driving-frequency controlled creation, motion, and annihilation of Floquet tensor monopoles, along with anomalous bulk-edge correspondence unique to the non-equilibrium regime.
conclusion: This work extends tensor monopole research to non-equilibrium systems, providing a platform for exploring exotic topological phases in dynamic tensor gauge fields and functional topological devices with real-time control.

title: A Less-for-more Metamaterial Paradigm Via Laplace-Helmholtz Correspondence
authors: Zihang Guo, Fubao Yang, Tong Li, Shuihua Yang, Cheng-Wei Qiu, Jingjing He And Liujun Xu
abstract: The Laplace and Helmholtz equations dominate two fundamentally distinct physical processes: steady diffusion with a single constitutive parameter versus dynamic wave propagation with two. Manipulating complex wave dynamics through simple steady fields is typically deemed infeasible. Here, we bridge this gap by establishing the Laplace-Helmholtz correspondence, enabling a ‘less-for-more’ paradigm for metamaterial design. Rooted in a wave invariant, this framework allows the rigorous derivation of the two parameters and oscillatory field for the Helmholtz equation (the ‘more’) solely from the single parameter and steady field of the Laplace equation (the ‘less’). We demonstrate this capability by unlocking functionalities previously considered intractable, such as hyperbolic invisibility and three-dimensional freeform conformal cloaking with broadband performance. We further experimentally validate our strategy via a waveguide cloak. Our results bridge static and dynamic physics, establishing a versatile gateway for manipulating waves beyond conventional constraints.
tldr: This paper establishes a mathematical correspondence between Laplace and Helmholtz equations to design metamaterials for wave manipulation using static diffusion fields.
motivation: To bridge the gap between static and dynamic physics, enabling complex wave functionalities (e.g., hyperbolic invisibility, 3D cloaking) through simpler steady-state design.
method: The authors derive a wave invariant that maps the single-parameter Laplace equation to the two-parameter Helmholtz equation, allowing wave parameters and fields to be obtained from static solutions.
result: They demonstrate hyperbolic invisibility and 3D freeform conformal cloaking with broadband performance, and experimentally validate a waveguide cloak.
conclusion: The Laplace-Helmholtz correspondence provides a versatile gateway for manipulating waves beyond conventional constraints, enabling a 'less-for-more' paradigm in metamaterial design.

title: Pseudo-Hermitian Magnon Dynamics
authors: Xi-Guang Wang And Jamal Berakdar
abstract: A defining quantity of a physical system is its energy which is represented by the Hamiltonian. In closed quantum mechanical or/and fully coherent wave-based systems the Hamiltonian is introduced as a Hermitian operator which ensures real energy spectrum and secures the decomposition of any state over a complete basis set that spans the space where states live. Pseudo-Hermitian, or PT symmetric, systems are a special class of non-Hermitian ones. They describe open systems but may still have real energy spectrum. The eigenmodes are however not orthogonal in general. This qualitative difference to Hermitian physics has a range of consequences for the physical behavior of the system in the steady state or when it is subjected to external perturbations. This overview reviews the recent progress in the field of pseudo-Hermitian physics as it unfolds when applied to low-energy excitations of magnetically ordered materials. The focus is mainly on long wavelength spin excitations (spin waves) with magnons being the energy quanta of these excitations. Various setups including ferromagnetic, antiferromagnetic, magnonic crystals, and hybrid structures with different types of coupling to the environments as well as spatio-temporally engineered systems will be discussed with a focus on the particular aspects that are brought about by the pseudo-Hermiticity such as mode amplification, non-reciprocal propagation, magnon cloaking, non-Hermitian skin effect, PT-symmetric assisted Floquet engineering, topological energy transfer, and field-induced enhanced sensitivity.
tldr: A review of pseudo-Hermitian magnon dynamics in magnetically ordered materials, focusing on non-Hermitian effects like mode amplification and non-reciprocal propagation.
motivation: To explore the unique physics of pseudo-Hermitian (PT-symmetric) systems in the context of magnon excitations, which offer new phenomena not present in Hermitian systems.
method: The paper reviews theoretical and experimental progress on pseudo-Hermitian magnonics, covering various setups such as ferromagnetic, antiferromagnetic, magnonic crystals, and hybrid structures.
result: Key phenomena include mode amplification, non-reciprocal propagation, magnon cloaking, non-Hermitian skin effect, PT-symmetric Floquet engineering, topological energy transfer, and enhanced sensitivity.
conclusion: Pseudo-Hermitian magnonics is a rapidly developing field with potential applications in spintronics and magnonics, but it is not directly aligned with the user's research interests in quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: A Comprehensive Review On Master Stability Functions In Complex Network Dynamics
authors: Priodyuti Pradhan And Chandrakala Meena Suman Acharyya
abstract: Synchronization is a fundamental emergent phenomenon observed across a wide range of natural and engineered systems. Understanding the stability of a synchronization phenomenon is crucial for ensuring functionality in various complex systems. The master stability function (MSF) framework has emerged as a powerful and elegant tool for analyzing the stability of synchronization in coupled dynamical systems. By separating the effects of the node dynamics from the network structure, the MSF offers deep insights into synchronization behavior. However, a major challenge lies in determining the MSF for complex dynamical networks driven by nonlinear interaction mechanisms. These mechanisms introduce additional complexity due to the intricate connectivity of the interacting elements and the complex dynamics governed by nonlinear processes, diverse parameters, and the higher dimensionality of the system. Although MSF analysis has been widely used for more than past 25 years, a comprehensive and systematic investigation of MSF across various networked systems is still lacking. In this article, we present a simplified and unified analysis for the MSF in various undirected and directed networked systems. We begin by formulating the MSF framework in pairwise coupled identical systems and extend our analysis to directed networks and multilayer networks, considering both intralayer and interlayer interactions. Furthermore, we analyze the MSF formalism for higher-order networks. To facilitate understanding, we complement the theoretical developments with numerical analysis of synchronization stability in coupled systems. We also propose algorithms for computing the MSF, identifying stability regimes, and classifying the MSF behaviors. Overall, the primary goal of this review is to present a systematic study of the MSF in various coupled dynamical networks in a clear and structured manner, making this powerful tool more accessible. Furthermore, we highlight underexplored areas in the application of the MSF and discuss emerging directions, such as estimating the MSF using machine learning approaches.
tldr: A comprehensive review of the master stability function framework for analyzing synchronization stability in complex networks, covering pairwise, directed, multilayer, and higher-order networks.
motivation: Synchronization is a key emergent phenomenon in natural and engineered systems, and understanding its stability is crucial. Despite 25 years of MSF analysis, a systematic and unified treatment across various network types is lacking.
method: The paper formulates the MSF framework for pairwise coupled identical systems, then extends to directed networks, multilayer networks (intra- and interlayer), and higher-order networks. Numerical simulations and algorithms for computing MSF and classifying stability regimes are provided.
result: A simplified and unified MSF analysis is presented for undirected, directed, multilayer, and higher-order networks, with numerical examples demonstrating stability regimes.
conclusion: The review systematizes MSF analysis across diverse network topologies, making the tool more accessible, and highlights underexplored areas and future directions such as machine learning-based MSF estimation.

title: Classification And Correlation Signatures Of Chiral Spin Liquids On The Pyrochlore Lattice
authors: Leon Balents And Yasir Iqbal Chunxiao Liu
abstract: We present a systematic classification and variational study of chiral quantum spin liquids on the pyrochlore lattice based on fermionic parton constructions. Focusing on chiral and spin-liquid Ansätze, we characterize their symmetry properties, flux structures, and low-energy spinon spectra within a projective symmetry group framework, and incorporate gauge fluctuations through Gutzwiller-projected wave functions studied by variational Monte Carlo. From the equal-time spin structure factor, we develop correlation-based diagnostics that distinguish gauge-dominated Coulomb phases from states with substantial matter-field and short-range contributions. Distinct chiral flux sectors, though close in energy, exhibit markedly different degrees of emergent gauge-field dominance, reflected in the geometry and contrast of pinch-point singularities. Although these states are not competitive ground states of the nearest-neighbor Heisenberg model, they define a physically meaningful family of proximate chiral phases relevant to extended pyrochlore Hamiltonians.
tldr: This paper classifies chiral spin liquids on the pyrochlore lattice using parton constructions and variational Monte Carlo, focusing on symmetry and correlation signatures.
motivation: Chiral spin liquids are exotic quantum phases with potential relevance to frustrated magnets, but their classification on the pyrochlore lattice is incomplete.
method: The authors use fermionic parton theory with projective symmetry groups to classify chiral Ansätze, and study Gutzwiller-projected wave functions via variational Monte Carlo to compute spin structure factors.
result: Distinct chiral flux sectors are identified, showing varying degrees of gauge-field dominance reflected in pinch-point singularities, though they are not ground states of the nearest-neighbor Heisenberg model.
conclusion: The work provides a family of proximate chiral phases for extended pyrochlore Hamiltonians, but does not directly advance quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Physical Sampling For Computational Photography
authors: Ni Chen And David J Brady
abstract: The standard model of photography is that lenses form images and focal planes capture those images. Over the past two decades, however, cameras have been transformed from devices that record focal images into analog-to-digital converters that transform massively parallel optical signals into serial electronic data. Under this new model, one may choose to maximize the quality and quantity of captured information, rather than focal image quality. Here we review the nature of the optical data stream and consider lens and focal plane designs that improve information capture capacity. After maximizing information capacity, the challenge of converting this information to digital data requires novel read-out and compression. We review strategies for approaching physical information limits under realistic size, power, and bandwidth constraints. Multiscale monocentric (spherical primary optics combined with arrays of secondary micro-cameras, each imaging a narrow subfield) and array lens architectures relax unfavorable geometric scaling by trading monolithic optics for co-designed system-level integration (jointly optimized optics, focal-plane, and readout subsystems). Metaoptic and mode-sorting focal plane filters implement richer projection operators that sample spectral, polarimetric, and coherence features without requiring exhaustive scanning. Finally, because readout and computation dominate energy at high throughput, we highlight architectures that perform dimensionality reduction before (or during) digitization, including integrated photonic encoders and multilayer optical projections coupled to detection and learned decoding. Together, these developments motivate a shift from cameras optimized to produce 2D images toward cameras engineered as end-to-end information channels, co-designing optics, focal-plane, and readout to deliver more task-relevant measurements per photon and per joule.
tldr: This paper reviews computational photography architectures that optimize information capture and readout under physical constraints, but does not address quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: The authors aim to shift camera design from producing 2D images to engineering end-to-end information channels, maximizing task-relevant measurements per photon and per joule.
method: The paper reviews multiscale monocentric optics, metaoptic filters, and integrated photonic encoders that perform dimensionality reduction before digitization.
result: It identifies architectures that improve information capacity and energy efficiency by co-designing optics, focal-plane, and readout subsystems.
conclusion: Future cameras should be designed as information channels rather than image recorders, leveraging co-design to overcome physical scaling limits.

motivation: Radioactive molecules offer unique opportunities for precision tests of fundamental symmetries and physics beyond the Standard Model, but their production has been challenging.

[Phys. Rev. B 114, 045203] Published Wed Jul 15, 2026.
tldr: This paper investigates the origin of acceptor preference (B vs Al) in silicon, diamond, and silicon carbide semiconductors.
motivation: Understanding why B is preferred in Si and diamond while Al is preferred in SiC is important for optimizing p-type doping in these materials.

result: The preference is attributed to differences in atomic size, electronegativity, and lattice relaxation effects.
conclusion: The study provides a theoretical explanation for the observed acceptor preferences, aiding in the design of better p-type semiconductors.

Electrical detection of magnetization dynamics in magnetic insulators underpins both fundamental studies of magnon transport and the development of low-loss magnonic devices. In heavy-metal/magnetic-insulator heterostructures, spin pumping and spin-torque ferromagnetic resonance (ST-FMR) are widely …

tldr: This paper disambiguates electrical detection signals in magnetic insulator/heavy-metal heterostructures, distinguishing spin pumping from spin-torque ferromagnetic resonance.
motivation: Electrical detection of magnetization dynamics in magnetic insulators is important for magnon transport studies and magnonic devices, but the underlying mechanisms (spin pumping vs. ST-FMR) are often conflated.
method: The authors perform systematic measurements on yttrium iron garnet (YIG)/Pt bilayers with varying geometries and use a theoretical model to separate the contributions from spin pumping and ST-FMR.
result: They identify distinct signatures that allow unambiguous discrimination between the two effects, clarifying the interpretation of previous experiments.
conclusion: The work provides a clear framework for interpreting electrical detection signals in magnetic insulator/heavy-metal systems, aiding future magnon transport research.

tldr: This paper presents a filtered Rayleigh-Ritz method and the Prony-Ritz equivalence class for extracting energy spectra from correlation functions in lattice quantum field theory.
motivation: Extracting excited-state energies from correlation functions is a longstanding challenge in lattice QCD, and recent Lanczos-based methods offer improvements but require careful analysis of numerical stability and equivalence.
method: The authors develop a filtered Rayleigh-Ritz method that uses a filter function to isolate eigenstates, and establish an equivalence class between Prony-like methods and Rayleigh-Ritz methods, showing that the Lanczos method is a special case.
result: They demonstrate that the filtered Rayleigh-Ritz method yields accurate energy spectra and matrix elements, and the Prony-Ritz equivalence class unifies several existing approaches.
conclusion: The work provides a rigorous framework for extracting spectral information from correlation functions, with implications for lattice QCD and other quantum field theory computations.

Athermal systems such as granular materials exhibit reproducible volume fluctuations despite the absence of thermal equilibration, yet a quantitative statistical-mechanical description remains incomplete. Within the Edwards ensemble, volume replaces energy as the conserved quantity and compactivity …

title: Colloquium: Multimessenger Astronomy With Continuous Gravitational Waves And Future Detectors
authors: Benjamin J. Owen
abstract:
Author(s): Benjamin J. Owen

The search for continuous gravitational waves from rotating neutron stars represents a key frontier of gravitational-wave astrophysics, with strong connections to electromagnetic astronomy, nuclear astrophysics, and condensed matter physics. This Colloquium discusses the detection prospects for these long-lived yet elusive signals in the upcoming generation of gravitational-wave detectors, emphasizing the importance of simultaneous electromagnetic observations. It also surveys the potential implications of such multimessenger observations for our understanding of the physical and astrophysical processes taking place in the extremely dense environments of their sources.

title: Prospects For Supersymmetry At High-Luminosity Lhc

abstract:

Supersymmetry remains one of the leading candidates for physics beyond the standard model, offering a compelling framework to address the hierarchy of scales. Its theoretical appeal has inspired decades of intensive model building and experimental searches. Recent results have placed stringent bounds on the supersymmetric parameter space, sharpening the focus on the remaining viable models. This review surveys the current status and outlook for supersymmetry in light of experimental constraints and recent theoretical developments, and presents projections for the discovery potential of the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider across multiple search channels and a variety of well-motivated scenarios.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045001] Published Fri Oct 17, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews the prospects for supersymmetry at the High-Luminosity LHC, summarizing experimental constraints and discovery potential.
motivation: Supersymmetry is a leading candidate for beyond Standard Model physics, and the HL-LHC offers a new opportunity to search for it.
method: The authors survey current experimental bounds and theoretical developments, and project discovery potential across multiple search channels.
result: Stringent bounds have narrowed viable parameter space, but the HL-LHC can still probe many well-motivated scenarios.
conclusion: Supersymmetry remains viable and the HL-LHC will provide crucial tests.

There are many nuclear reactions that are of central importance for stellar burning and element formation. In typical stars, these reactions take place at very low energy, and many of them have very small rates, making it difficult to measure them directly in the laboratory. On the theoretical side, the low-energy regime is governed by quantum-mechanical phenomena like tunneling, near-threshold resonances, and interference effects. This review summarizes the state of the art in the theory of low-energy nuclear reactions in stars and describes new ideas for studying these reactions on Earth.

title: Self-aligning Polar Active Matter
authors: Paul Baconnier, Olivier Dauchot, Vincent Démery, Gustavo Düring, Silke Henkes, Cristián Huepe, And Amir Shee
abstract:
Author(s): Paul Baconnier, Olivier Dauchot, Vincent Démery, Gustavo Düring, Silke Henkes, Cristián Huepe, and Amir Shee

What if active units could align–or even antialign–their orientation with their own velocity? This intriguing self-alignment property unlocks a spectrum of fascinating behaviors, from single self-propelled particles orbiting in harmonic traps to transformative collective phenomena like synchronized motion in dense or solid elastic assemblies. Unlike systems where units simply mimic their neighbors, self-alignment fundamentally reshapes how motion emerges, paving the way for groundbreaking discoveries in biology, smart materials, and robotics. This review uncovers the hidden power of self-alignment in active systems, introduces a unified mathematical and conceptual framework, explores existing models of self-alignment, and highlights its transformative impact on the study and real-world applications of active systems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015007] Published Thu Mar 20, 2025.
tldr: A review of self-alignment in polar active matter, covering its role in collective motion and potential applications in biology and robotics.
motivation: To understand how self-alignment, where active units align their orientation with their velocity, leads to novel collective behaviors and to provide a unified framework for studying such systems.
method: The paper reviews existing models and experiments on self-alignment in active matter, synthesizing them into a unified mathematical and conceptual framework.
result: Self-alignment enables phenomena such as orbiting in harmonic traps and synchronized motion in dense assemblies, with implications for smart materials and robotics.
conclusion: Self-alignment is a fundamental property that reshapes motion in active systems, offering a new perspective for future discoveries and applications.

abstract:
Author(s): Ludwig Englert, Dominik Jüstel, and Vasilis Ntziachristos

Advanced imaging methods are essential for providing biological and clinical insight into cells and biological tissues. Optoacoustic imaging is one such method in which cells or tissues absorb short laser pulses and the resulting rise in temperature creates tiny ultrasound waves that can be detected by ultrasonic detectors placed outside the specimen. This noninvasive technique has the ability to look at optical contrast that is millimeters and even centimeters deep with high resolution. This review discusses the basic physics, how the method impacts biological and clinical research, and the latest developments in multimodal microscopy and imaging combining optical and optoacoustic techniques.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015005] Published Tue Mar 04, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews optoacoustic microscopy, a biomedical imaging technique that uses laser pulses to generate ultrasound waves for deep-tissue imaging.

method: The review covers the basic physics of optoacoustic imaging, its impact on biological and clinical research, and recent developments in multimodal microscopy combining optical and optoacoustic techniques.
result: Optoacoustic microscopy enables imaging of optical contrast at millimeter-to-centimeter depths with high resolution, and multimodal approaches enhance its capabilities.
conclusion: Optoacoustic microscopy is a valuable tool for biological and clinical imaging, with ongoing developments in multimodal systems.

title: Advancing Science By Designing For Surprise | Science
abstract: Consider a thought experiment. Two graduate students have written identical dissertations: the same experiments, the same data, the same robust findings. The other reframes the study for a different, but equally relevant, audience—one holding different suppositions and therefore open to being surprised into shifting its position. The latter approach is more valuable for good reasons: the scientific community and the world will learn more.
tldr: The paper discusses the value of designing scientific studies to surprise audiences with different assumptions, rather than presenting novel technical results.

title: Social Calibration Of Sycophantic AI—Response | Science
abstract: We thank Meng for articulating important methodological and interpretive questions about our findings. The appropriate human baseline depends on the expected social role of artificial intelligence (AI). In real-world use, AI models are perceived to serve a variety of purposes, such as adviser, neutral outside opinion, editor, and assistant (1, 2). These roles come with different expectations for how often agreement, validation, or corrective feedback should occur. To complicate matters, users often view a single AI system as fulfilling multiple roles (3, 4). Because of the ambiguity of AI’s social role, any single human baseline is an imperfect comparison point. The baselines we used—judgments from third-party humans with no personal stake in the conflict or scenario at hand—explore one common and societally meaningful expectation: Do AI systems—despite often being seen as external, neutral, and objective information providers (5–7)—disproportionately side with the user? Our findings were also robust to an alternative baseline of online crowdworker judgments (supplementary materials, SM 2). Responses from those with closer relationships to the advice-seeker may indeed be shaped by stronger relational norms, reputational accountability, and lasting social consequences. Whether such alternatives would result in more or less divergence remains an open question.
tldr: This paper discusses the social calibration of sycophantic AI responses, focusing on human baselines and expectations of AI's social role.
motivation: The authors respond to methodological questions about their study on AI sycophancy, aiming to clarify the appropriate human baseline for comparison.
method: They argue that the appropriate baseline depends on AI's perceived social role (e.g., adviser, editor) and show robustness using alternative baselines like online crowdworkers.
result: The findings suggest that AI systems disproportionately side with users compared to neutral third-party human judges, but the divergence may vary with relational context.
conclusion: The ambiguity of AI's social role makes any single human baseline imperfect, and further research is needed to understand how relational norms affect expectations.

title: Social Calibration Of Sycophantic Ai | Science
abstract: In their Research Article “Sycophantic AI decreases prosocial intentions and promotes dependence” (26 March, 10.1126/science. aec8352), M. Cheng et al. show that artificial intelligence (AI) systems are substantially more likely than humans to endorse a user’s position in disputed scenarios. Randomized experimental designs indicate that exposure to such affirming responses reduces users’ willingness to engage in prosocial corrective actions in interpersonal conflicts and increases trust in, and dependence on, the AI system. These findings, which establish a causal link between model alignment strategies and downstream human behavior, highlight a tension at the heart of AI alignment: Optimizing for user satisfaction may systematically bias models toward agreement, even when disagreement would better serve users’ long-term interests or social outcomes. Sycophancy is not merely a failure mode but a predictable by-product of reinforcement signals derived from user preference. However, methodological and interpretive questions remain.
tldr: This paper studies sycophantic behavior in AI systems and its impact on human prosocial behavior, which is unrelated to quantum information theory.
motivation: The paper investigates how AI alignment strategies that optimize for user satisfaction can lead to sycophantic responses, affecting user behavior and trust.
method: The authors use randomized experimental designs to compare AI and human responses in disputed scenarios and measure downstream effects on users' prosocial intentions and dependence.
result: AI systems are more likely to endorse user positions, reducing users' willingness to engage in prosocial corrective actions and increasing dependence on the AI.
conclusion: Sycophancy is a predictable byproduct of reinforcement signals from user preference, highlighting a tension in AI alignment between user satisfaction and long-term social outcomes.

result: They find that the spin polarization of protons can be extracted from hypertriton measurements, offering a new probe of the plasma's vortical structure.
conclusion: The study contributes to heavy-ion physics and the understanding of the quark-gluon plasma, but does not relate to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

Super-resonance maintains a broadband out-of-phase response well beyond the characteristic bandwidth of conventional resonance, enabling broadband flow stabilization among other applications.

method: The authors theoretically propose and experimentally demonstrate a super-resonance phenomenon that maintains a broadband out-of-phase response beyond the characteristic bandwidth of conventional resonance.

title: Colloquium: What Do We Mean By ‘active Matter’?
authors: Michael Te Vrugt, Benno Liebchen, And Michael E. Cates
abstract:
Author(s): Michael te Vrugt, Benno Liebchen, and Michael E. Cates

Active matter has become a lively topic in recent years, but what exactly is meant by the term ‘active matter’ is often unclear. This Colloquium discusses the scientific and semantic issues underlying this ambiguity, as well as the history of the field, and offers a definition of active matter as a well-defined subset of nonequilibrium systems. It then surveys recent developments including nonreciprocal interactions, intracellular phase separation, and quantum active matter.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 031001] Published Mon Jul 13, 2026.
tldr: This Colloquium discusses the definition and scope of active matter as a subset of nonequilibrium systems, including recent developments like nonreciprocal interactions and quantum active matter.
motivation: The term 'active matter' is often used ambiguously; the paper aims to clarify its meaning and provide a precise definition.
method: The authors review the history of the field, analyze semantic issues, and propose a definition based on a well-defined subset of nonequilibrium systems.
result: They offer a definition of active matter and survey recent developments including nonreciprocal interactions, intracellular phase separation, and quantum active matter.
conclusion: Active matter is a distinct class of nonequilibrium systems, and the proposed definition helps unify the field.

title: Tip-enhanced Molecular Fluorescence Microscopy With Atomic-scale Resolution
authors: Anna Rosławska, Katharina Kaiser, Sofia Canola, Song Jiang, Fabrice Scheurer, Javier Aizpurua, Tomáš Neuman, And Guillaume Schull
abstract:
Author(s): Anna Rosławska, Katharina Kaiser, Sofia Canola, Song Jiang, Fabrice Scheurer, Javier Aizpurua, Tomáš Neuman, and Guillaume Schull

Scanning probe techniques have transformed our ability to study materials at the atomic scale, providing atom-by-atom views of surfaces. Tip-enhanced molecular fluorescence microscopy combines scanning probes with optical fluorescence. Such optical techniques normally have spatial resolution limited by the wavelength of the light used. However, using the scanning tip itself as a nanoscale optical antenna confines the electromagnetic field to the tip apex, achieving superresolution down to the atomic scale. Fluorescence is a fundamental probe of materials that reveals electronic structure and vibronic properties by exciting electrons to higher levels and observing the photons emitted when they relax. These capabilities are of particular interest for studying and identifying molecules, submolecular structures, and their reactions. This review discusses the techniques of tip-enhanced molecular fluorescence microscopy and the new insights they have revealed.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025007] Published Tue Jun 30, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews tip-enhanced molecular fluorescence microscopy achieving atomic-scale resolution, a scanning probe technique for studying molecular electronic and vibronic properties.
motivation: To overcome the diffraction limit in optical microscopy and achieve atomic-scale spatial resolution for studying individual molecules and their submolecular structures.
method: The technique uses a scanning probe tip as a nanoscale optical antenna to confine the electromagnetic field at the tip apex, enabling super-resolution fluorescence imaging.
result: Atomic-scale resolution is achieved in fluorescence microscopy, allowing the study of electronic structure and vibronic properties of individual molecules.
conclusion: Tip-enhanced molecular fluorescence microscopy provides a powerful tool for nanoscale optical characterization of molecules, with potential applications in chemistry and materials science.

title: High-energy Emission From The Galactic Center
authors: Andrea Goldwurm, Maïca Clavel, Stefano Gabici, And Régis Terrier
abstract:
Author(s): Andrea Goldwurm, Maïca Clavel, Stefano Gabici, and Régis Terrier

In this review, the authors provide a comprehensive multiwavelength view of high-energy emission from the center of our Galaxy. This region contains the closest supermassive black hole to us, which offers the best studied galactic nucleus in the Universe, with its quiescent emission and accretion contrasted by flaring activity. The Galactic Center also hosts diverse compact sources, plasma bubbles, and x-ray chimneys, altogether forming a dense interacting molecular zone—a gigantic powerhouse in the Milky Way.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025006] Published Mon Jun 29, 2026.
tldr: A review of high-energy emission from the Galactic Center, covering the supermassive black hole, compact sources, and plasma bubbles.
motivation: To provide a comprehensive multiwavelength view of the high-energy phenomena in the Galactic Center region.
method: Review of observational data across multiple wavelengths.
result: Summarizes the current understanding of the Galactic Center's high-energy emission and its sources.
conclusion: The Galactic Center is a unique laboratory for studying high-energy astrophysical processes.

title: Fundamentals Of Vacuum Breakdown In High-gradient Accelerator Structures
authors: Walter Wuensch, Sergio Calatroni, Flyura Djurabekova, Andreas Kyritsakis, And Yinon Ashkenazy
abstract:
Author(s): Walter Wuensch, Sergio Calatroni, Flyura Djurabekova, Andreas Kyritsakis, and Yinon Ashkenazy

Vacuum breakdown or arcing happens when a very strong electric field causes a metal surface in a vacuum to suddenly form plasma, allowing large electrical currents to flow. Breakdown can damage particle accelerators, fusion reactors, satellites, and x-ray devices, though it is useful in technologies like plasma thrusters. Scientists have studied this unpredictable and fast phenomenon for over a century. Recent advances in experiments and computer simulations now provide a coherent mechanistic picture: tiny surface defects, electrical stress, heat, and emitted particles interact in complex ways to trigger breakdowns. These insights could improve high-power technologies and make advanced accelerators more reliable and efficient.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025004] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews the physics of vacuum breakdown in high-gradient accelerator structures, focusing on the role of surface defects, electrical stress, and plasma formation.
motivation: Vacuum breakdown limits the performance of particle accelerators and other high-power devices; understanding its mechanism is crucial for improving reliability and efficiency.
method: The authors synthesize experimental observations and computer simulations to build a coherent mechanistic picture of the breakdown process.
result: They identify that tiny surface defects, electrical stress, heat, and emitted particles interact in complex ways to trigger breakdowns.
conclusion: These insights can guide the design of more robust accelerator structures and other high-power technologies.

title: Colloquium: Hadron Production In Open-charm Meson Pairs At ${e}^{+}{e}^{−}$ Colliders
authors: Xiongfei Wang, Xiang Liu, And Yuanning Gao
abstract:
Author(s): Xiongfei Wang, Xiang Liu, and Yuanning Gao

Hadron spectroscopy is a frontier of particle physics; searching for new hadrons is crucial for validating the theory of strong interaction (QCD). Investigating how charmonium, a bound state of charm and anticharm quarks, decays and searching for new charmoniumlike states yield valuable insights into strong interaction mechanisms, including quark confinement and gluon binding. Hadrons produced at e− collisions decaying to open-charm meson pairs are a primary source of experimental information for these investigations. This Colloquium reviews current progress from BARBAR, Belle, CLEO-c, and BESIII experiments. As BESIII accumulates high-precision data, it has emerged as the leading facility for measuring hadron production in charm-meson pair systems, and recent advances are highlighted.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 021001] Published Fri Apr 03, 2026.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews experimental progress in hadron production from open-charm meson pairs at e+e- colliders, focusing on charmonium spectroscopy and strong interaction mechanisms.
motivation: Understanding charmonium decays and searching for new hadrons are crucial for validating quantum chromodynamics (QCD) and exploring quark confinement and gluon binding.
method: The paper reviews experimental results from BARBAR, Belle, CLEO-c, and BESIII experiments on hadron production in e+e- collisions decaying to open-charm meson pairs.
result: BESIII has emerged as the leading facility for high-precision measurements in this area, and recent advances are highlighted.
conclusion: The review summarizes current knowledge and emphasizes the importance of ongoing experimental efforts in hadron spectroscopy.

authors: Véronique van Elewyck And Dietrich Belitz
abstract:
Author(s): Véronique Van Elewyck and Dietrich Belitz

Three Colloquia honor the Arecibo Observatory’s legacy, exploring its revolutionary impact on planetary radar studies, radio astronomy, and geospace science.

motivation: To honor the Arecibo Observatory's contributions to science.
method: Colloquia and editorial summary.
result: Highlights the observatory's impact across multiple fields.
conclusion: The Arecibo Observatory had a revolutionary impact on planetary radar, radio astronomy, and geospace science.

title: Colloquium: Planetary Radar At The Arecibo Observatory
authors: Michael C. Nolan, Lynn M. Carter, And Edgard G. Rivera-Valentín
abstract:
Author(s): Michael C. Nolan, Lynn M. Carter, and Edgard G. Rivera-Valentín

For more than two decades, the planetary radar installed at the Arecibo Telescope was the most sensitive instrument of its kind, harnessing the penetrating power of radio waves to perform observations of the (sub)surface of planets, moons, and asteroids in the Solar System—providing a unique perspective on those bodies that helped to drive in situ exploration. This Colloquium presents an overview of the scientific legacy of the Arecibo radar system, focusing on the period posterior to the Gregorian Update in the late 1990s until the unexpected demise of the telescope in 2020. After recalling the basics of planetary radar techniques, it reviews key Arecibo observations of Mercury, Venus, Mars, our Moon, and the Saturn system, and highlights its essential role in the characterization of a large sample of near-Earth asteroids and comets.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011003] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews the scientific legacy of planetary radar observations at the Arecibo Observatory, focusing on Solar System bodies.
motivation: Planetary radar provides unique subsurface and surface information about planets, moons, and asteroids, complementing in situ exploration.
method: The paper summarizes the basics of planetary radar techniques and reviews key Arecibo observations of Mercury, Venus, Mars, the Moon, the Saturn system, and near-Earth asteroids.
result: Arecibo's radar system was the most sensitive of its kind for over two decades, enabling detailed characterization of many Solar System objects.
conclusion: The Arecibo radar system made significant contributions to planetary science, and its loss marks the end of an era for ground-based planetary radar.

title: Colloquium: Radio Astronomy With The Arecibo 305-m Telescope: In Contemporaneous Context
authors: Tapasi Ghosh And Chris Salter
abstract:
Author(s): Tapasi Ghosh and Chris Salter

The Arecibo Observatory, inaugurated in 1963 as the world’s largest single-dish radio telescope, remained at the forefront of astronomy and atmospheric science for more than five decades, until its catastrophic collapse in December 2020. This Colloquium focuses on Arecibo’s enduring legacy in radio astronomy, offering a historical perspective that emphasizes how successive major upgrades of the telescope continuously expanded its observational capabilities and scientific impact. It presents Arecibo’s most influential contributions in topics as diverse as pulsar studies, the mapping of neutral hydrogen (HI) in the Milky Way and other galaxies, the characterization of the interstellar medium, the imaging of extragalactic radio sources with very long baseline interferometry (VLBI), the search for extraterrestrial intelligence (SETI), and being a major contributor to the first-ever detection of a stochastic gravitational-wave background.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011004] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: This paper is a historical review of radio astronomy contributions made by the Arecibo 305-m telescope.
motivation: To document the scientific legacy of the Arecibo Observatory in radio astronomy following its collapse.
method: Historical narrative and summary of key observational achievements across multiple subfields.
result: Highlights Arecibo's major contributions to pulsar studies, HI mapping, VLBI, SETI, and gravitational-wave background detection.
conclusion: Arecibo's upgrades and long operational life enabled a wide range of influential radio astronomy discoveries.

title: Colloquium: Geospace Pathfinder Science At Arecibo Observatory
authors: J. D. Mathews, M. P. Sulzer, And Shikha Raizada
abstract:
Author(s): J. D. Mathews, M. P. Sulzer, and Shikha Raizada

The Arecibo Observatory housed the largest single-aperture radio telescope for approximately 50 years. A major scientific focus was studying the upper atmosphere; its highly sensitive radar facility, combined with lidars, optical sensors, and satellite-based systems, enabled unprecedented studies of ionospheric physics based on incoherent scattering of radio waves off free electrons. After establishing the fundamental concepts and observables of the incoherent scattering radar technique, this Colloquium reviews key advances obtained with the Arecibo suite of instruments in multiple areas of geospace science, including plasma physics, space weather, lidar studies of atomic metals in the ionosphere, and ionosphere-magnetosphere coupling.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011005] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews geospace science advances made using the Arecibo Observatory's radar and lidar instruments, focusing on ionospheric physics and space weather.
motivation: The Arecibo Observatory's unique capabilities for studying the upper atmosphere have led to significant insights in plasma physics and space weather, but this work is unrelated to quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: The paper is a colloquium review summarizing key results from incoherent scatter radar, lidar, and optical measurements of the ionosphere and magnetosphere.
result: It highlights advances in understanding ionospheric plasma processes, metal layers, and coupling between the ionosphere and magnetosphere.
conclusion: The Arecibo Observatory has been a vital tool for geospace research, but the paper does not address quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Colloquium: Convection-cloud Chambers: Experiment And Theory
authors: Steven Krueger And Raymond A. Shaw
abstract:
Author(s): Steven Krueger and Raymond A. Shaw

In warm clouds, drops grow into raindrops through both condensation and collision coalescence, but the observed rapid transition between these mechanisms remains difficult to theoretically explain. The convection-cloud chamber, which reproduces key phenomena such as turbulent fluctuations in droplet concentrations and supersaturation under controlled laboratory conditions, offers a promising approach to addressing this long-standing bottleneck in understanding in cloud physics. This Colloquium reviews the physics underlying the precipitation bottleneck, examines how convection-cloud chambers capture the essential processes, and synthesizes insights from experiments, theory, and computational models that bridge laboratory and atmospheric scales.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011001] Published Wed Feb 04, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews convection-cloud chambers as a laboratory tool to study the precipitation bottleneck in warm clouds.
motivation: Understanding the rapid transition from condensation to collision-coalescence in warm clouds is a long-standing problem in cloud physics.
method: The paper synthesizes insights from experiments, theory, and computational models of convection-cloud chambers.
result: Convection-cloud chambers reproduce key phenomena such as turbulent fluctuations in droplet concentrations and supersaturation, offering a controlled environment to study cloud processes.
conclusion: The convection-cloud chamber is a promising approach to bridge laboratory and atmospheric scales and address the precipitation bottleneck.

title: Colloquium: Gravitational Waves From Neutrino-driven Core Collapse Supernovae
authors: A. Mezzacappa And M. Zanolin
abstract:
Author(s): A. Mezzacappa and M. Zanolin

The observation of a core collapse supernova explosion of (near-)Galactic origin would constitute a landmark, once-in-a-century event for multimessenger astronomy, eagerly awaited by observers and modelers alike. The detection of gravitational waves, along with photons and neutrinos, from such an event would provide unique insights into the supernova central engine and the physics of the newly forming neutron star. This Colloquium presents the latest progress in core collapse supernova modeling and the associated gravitational wave signal predictions. It also provides an overview of the specific methods of detection and physical parameter estimation that can be implemented for such signals in ground-based laser interferometers, in the context of multimessenger research strategies.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 041002] Published Tue Dec 30, 2025.
tldr: This colloquium reviews gravitational wave signals from core collapse supernovae and their detection methods.
motivation: Observing a Galactic core collapse supernova would be a landmark event for multimessenger astronomy, providing insights into the supernova engine and neutron star physics.
method: The paper summarizes progress in supernova modeling and gravitational wave signal predictions, and discusses detection and parameter estimation methods for ground-based laser interferometers.
result: The review presents the latest modeling results and signal predictions, but does not introduce new results.
conclusion: Gravitational wave detection from supernovae is a key multimessenger strategy, but the paper is a review without novel contributions to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Colloquium: The Cosmic Dipole Anomaly
authors: Nathan Secrest, Sebastian von Hausegger, Mohamed Rameez, Roya Mohayaee, And Subir Sarkar
abstract:
Author(s): Nathan Secrest, Sebastian von Hausegger, Mohamed Rameez, Roya Mohayaee, and Subir Sarkar

The cosmological principle, which states that the Universe must be statistically isotropic and homogeneous on large scales, is a foundational principle of the standard model of cosmology, known as lambda cold dark matter (ΛCDM). The validity of this principle can be tested by assessing the compatibility of a dipole anisotropy in the large-scale distribution of matter with the dipole observed in the cosmic microwave background, interpreted in the ΛCDM model as due to our local peculiar motion. This Colloquium describes the methodology for such a test and presents its outcome based on the analysis of recent large catalogs of radio galaxies and quasars, revealing a significant inconsistency between the two dipoles. The authors review these recent findings, as well as potential biases, systematic issues, and alternate interpretations, and discuss how this anomaly could challenge the standard description of our Universe based on the ΛCDM model.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 041001] Published Thu Dec 11, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews the cosmic dipole anomaly, a potential challenge to the cosmological principle and ΛCDM model, based on large-scale structure surveys.
motivation: To test the cosmological principle by comparing the dipole anisotropy in the distribution of radio galaxies and quasars with the cosmic microwave background dipole.
method: Analysis of recent large catalogs of radio galaxies and quasars to measure the dipole in the matter distribution and compare it with the CMB dipole.
result: A significant inconsistency is found between the two dipoles, suggesting a possible violation of the cosmological principle.
conclusion: The cosmic dipole anomaly may challenge the standard ΛCDM model, but further investigation of biases and systematics is needed.

title: Astrophysical Tests Of Dark Matter Self-interactions
authors: Susmita Adhikari, Arka Banerjee, Kimberly K. Boddy, Francis-Yan Cyr-Racine, Harry Desmond, Cora Dvorkin, Bhuvnesh Jain, Felix Kahlhoefer, Manoj Kaplinghat, Anna Nierenberg, Annika H. G. Peter, Andrew Robertson, Jeremy Sakstein, And Jesús Zavala
abstract:
Author(s): Susmita Adhikari, Arka Banerjee, Kimberly K. Boddy, Francis-Yan Cyr-Racine, Harry Desmond, Cora Dvorkin, Bhuvnesh Jain, Felix Kahlhoefer, Manoj Kaplinghat, Anna Nierenberg, Annika H. G. Peter, Andrew Robertson, Jeremy Sakstein, and Jesús Zavala

Dark sectors, involving new particles that couple very weakly to the standard model ones, play an important role in current model-building efforts in particle physics, as they allow, for example, for new dark matter production and interaction mechanisms. This review focuses on self-interacting dark matter scenarios, their implications on the dynamics and distribution of dark matter halos in the Universe, and the related astrophysical tests and observations, from galaxies to large-scale structures. It is embedded in the framework of the Novel Probes Project, a forum connecting observers and theorists involved in the study of astrophysical tests of dark-sector interactions.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045004] Published Mon Dec 08, 2025.
tldr: A review of astrophysical tests of self-interacting dark matter, focusing on dark matter halo dynamics and large-scale structure.
motivation: To understand the implications of self-interacting dark matter scenarios on galaxy formation and structure, and to summarize observational tests.
method: Review of theoretical models and comparison with astrophysical observations from galaxies to large-scale structures.
result: Summarizes current constraints on dark matter self-interaction cross-sections from various astrophysical probes.
conclusion: Self-interacting dark matter remains a viable candidate, with ongoing and future observations expected to further constrain its properties.

title: Solar Fusion Iii: New Data And Theory For Hydrogen-burning Stars
authors: B. Acharya et Al.
abstract:
Author(s): B. Acharya et al.

Approximately 90% of the stars in the Milky Way are on the main sequence, fusing hydrogen into helium through a network of nuclear reactions. This includes the nearest star, our Sun. A precise understanding of hydrogen burning is crucial to predicting its luminosity, neutrino production, and helioseismology. This review describes the theoretical and experimental work of the last decade that has advanced our understanding of the nuclear physics of hydrogen burning. It describes the plasma and atomic physics that influences the solar environment in which the nuclear reactions take place, as well as the diagnostics probes—including solar neutrinos and helioseismology—that allow us to test our resulting model of the solar interior.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 035002] Published Thu Sep 04, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews nuclear physics of hydrogen burning in stars, focusing on solar fusion and neutrino production.
motivation: Understanding hydrogen burning is crucial for predicting stellar luminosity, neutrino production, and helioseismology.
method: The review summarizes theoretical and experimental advances in nuclear reaction rates, plasma physics, and solar modeling.
result: Updated nuclear reaction rates and improved solar models are presented, with comparisons to neutrino and helioseismic data.

title: Gas Bubble Dynamics
authors: Dominique Legendre And Roberto Zenit
abstract:
Author(s): Dominique Legendre and Roberto Zenit

The motion of gas bubbles in liquids plays a vital role in numerous natural, industrial, and everyday phenomena. Unlike solid particles, gas bubbles are nearly weightless and highly responsive to forces from the surrounding fluid. Their dynamics are affected by added mass acceleration and deformable surfaces, and also by interactions with turbulent flows, other bubbles, and walls, with liquid rheology and surfactants further influencing their behavior. This review examines the intricate behavior of noncondensable gas bubbles, highlighting key advances over the past 20 years. Key topics include turbulence, non-Newtonian fluids, and electrolytes, offering insights to enhance modeling and guide future research in two-phase flow systems.

result: It highlights the effects of turbulence, liquid rheology, and surfactants on bubble behavior.
conclusion: The review provides insights to enhance modeling and guide future research in two-phase flow systems, but has no relevance to quantum information theory or related fields.
